rv.q: Alas, the resultant show, premiering at Writers Theatre in Glencoe, is a jumbled and confounding clunker.
“Wife of a Salesman” stands on its own.
Ultimately, the play’s effect is ambiguous; it echoes the despair of Miller’s classic but offers some tenuous hope.
Its world premier, running through April 3 at Writers Theatre in Glencoe, IL, is a theatrical event of the first order.
Eleanor Burgess has written another exciting play proving that she wasn’t a one-shot wonder.
Burgess' shrewd, multilayered play is about more than the madonna and the whore “duking it out,” as one character puts it.
One might reasonably call Wife of a Salesman a feminist play.
Still, one thing is for sure; you can’t question it’s a well-written play with great performances, besides my trepidation of the interruptions between scenes.
Fry and Drinkall ingeniously coalesce, displaying an understanding for each other and their characters self-worth, that leads to a remarkably theatrical, and most unexpected, outcome.
Burgess’s dramatic horizons expand, ending with a shock.
The unvarnished emotional truth Fry displays in this moment brings The Wife's suppressed despair into line with Blanche's willful delusion in 'A Streetcar Named Desire.'

And if the play can’t fully deliver on all the premises it promises, it’s still a heady, funny, and pointed portrait of two women determined to talk things over, even if societal expectations tell them that’s not an interesting or valid choice.
The play is remarkable, thought-provoking, and surprising, and the strength of the acting and design combine with the whip-smart text to create something truly worthwhile.
This is a brilliant work that takes us to a place we have never dared visit.

cn.t: Burgess's feminist reimagining of "Death of a Salesman" draws mostly strong praise for its clever premise and complex female characters, though one major dissenter finds it a confounding misfire.
